blocks.title: What is this file?
blocks.what: A Service gives a group of Pods one stable name and address. It comes from the core v1 API.
blocks.why: Pods come and go and get new addresses. A Service stays put, so other apps can always find yours.
blocks.ifRemoved: Kubernetes rejects the file, because it cannot tell what you want to create.
blocks.comment: What to create: a Service, from the core v1 API

blocks.title: Give it a name
blocks.what: This Service is called web. The name also becomes its address inside the cluster.
blocks.why: Other apps reach the Pods by asking for web, so pick a name that says what it serves.
blocks.ifRemoved: Kubernetes rejects the file, because every object needs a name.
blocks.comment: The name apps use to reach the Pods
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web

blocks.title: Which Pods?
blocks.what: The selector picks every Pod labelled app: web, the Pods from the Deployment lesson.
blocks.why: This is how a Service finds its Pods. It keeps the list up to date as Pods are replaced.
blocks.ifRemoved: The Service has no Pods to send traffic to, so requests fail.
blocks.comment: Send traffic to Pods labelled app: web
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  selector:
    app: web

blocks.title: Which ports?
blocks.what: The Service listens on port, then forwards each request to targetPort on a Pod.
blocks.why: The two can differ, so the Service can keep port 80 while the app listens elsewhere.
blocks.ifRemoved: Kubernetes rejects the Service, because it must say which port to listen on.
blocks.comment: Listen on port 80 and forward to port 80 on the Pods
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80

blocks.title: Inside the cluster only
blocks.what: ClusterIP gives the Service an address that works only inside the cluster. It is the default type.
blocks.why: Most apps only talk to each other, so they need nothing more. Writing it makes the choice clear.
blocks.ifRemoved: Nothing changes, because ClusterIP is the default.
blocks.comment: Reachable only from inside the cluster
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80
  type: ClusterIP

notes.apiVersion: The API group and version that define this kind. Services are in the core v1 API.
notes.kind: The type of object to create. A Service gives Pods one stable name and address.
notes.metadata: Details that identify the object, such as its name.
notes.spec: The desired state: which Pods to send traffic to, and on which ports.
notes.spec.selector: The labels a Pod must have to receive traffic from this Service.
notes.spec.selector.app: Send traffic to Pods labelled app: web, the Pods from the Deployment lesson.
notes.spec.ports: The ports the Service listens on. Each list item is one port.
notes.spec.ports[].protocol: The network protocol. TCP is the default and suits web traffic.
notes.spec.ports[].port: The port the Service listens on.
notes.spec.ports[].targetPort: The port on the Pods where the Service forwards each request. nginx listens on 80.
notes.metadata.name: The Service name. Pods in the same namespace can reach it by this name.
notes.spec.type: ClusterIP, the default, gives an address that works only inside the cluster.

tryIt.result: Starts the two web Pods from the Keep your app running lesson.
TYPE shows ClusterIP with a CLUSTER-IP address. EXTERNAL-IP shows <none>.
ENDPOINTS lists the addresses of both web Pods. The Service sends traffic there.
Prints the nginx welcome page, fetched by name from a short-lived Pod inside the cluster.
Removes the Service and the Deployment.

questions.question: Which Pods receive traffic from this Service?
questions.explain: The selector picks Pods by their labels. Pod names do not matter.

questions.question: What is the difference between port and targetPort?
answers: port is where the Service listens. targetPort is where the Pod listens.
port is on your laptop. targetPort is in the cluster.
They are two names for the same thing.
questions.explain: The Service receives on port and forwards to targetPort. Here both are 80.

questions.question: Can you open the CLUSTER-IP address in your laptop’s browser?
answers: No, a ClusterIP address works only inside the cluster
Only after you add a label
questions.explain: ClusterIP is for traffic between apps in the cluster. Later lessons open apps to the outside.

fix.explain: Labels are case-sensitive. Web does not match the Pods’ label web, so the Service finds no Pods.
fix.fix: Match the label exactly: app: web.
